Encode a DateTime into Eight Characters with base32 in Rust

July 2026

Overview

This is now I'm converting a DateTime from chrono into an eight character base32 string. The timestamps have a resolution of one second (i.e. no fractions of a second). I use these for the IDs for pages on my site. Each ID is split into four directories of two characters each. This prevents issues with too many items in a single directory causing issues.

Rust

[package]
name = "base32_timestamp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
chrono = "0.4.45"
data-encoding = "2.11.0"
use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
use data_encoding::BASE32_NOPAD;

fn main() {
  let dt = encode_datetime();
  let seconds_from_epoch = decode_datetime(&dt);
  println!("{}", dt);
  println!("{}", seconds_from_epoch);
}

fn encode_datetime() -> String {
  let dt: i64 = Utc::now().timestamp();
  let bytes = &dt.to_be_bytes()[3..8];
  BASE32_NOPAD.encode(bytes).to_lowercase().to_string()
}

fn decode_datetime(dt: &str) -> DateTime<Utc> {
  let five_bytes =
    BASE32_NOPAD.decode(dt.to_uppercase().as_bytes()).unwrap();
  let mut buf = [0u8; 8];
  buf[3..8].copy_from_slice(&five_bytes);
  let ts = i64::from_be_bytes(buf);
  DateTime::from_timestamp(ts, 0).unwrap()
}

Output

abvfvacc
2026-07-17 19:19:30 UTC

Endnotes

  • base32 encoding uses 32 characters where each one represents 5 bits.

  • 5 bits x 8 characters = 40 bits of data.

  • 40 bits (2^40) represents a little over 1 trillion values.

  • At 1 second per value, the 40 bits represents about 34,000 years. More than enough to cover the expected time I'll be posting on my blog.

  • The &dt.to_be_bytes()[3..8] call keeps the output lined up chronologically (by making it Big Endian, which I only half way understand), and strips of the first few bits from the byte which aren't needed.
